title: Design a Stock Exchange / Matching Engine
prompt: Design a stock exchange matching engine: clients submit limit and market orders for a set of instruments, the engine matches buyers and sellers by price-time priority, and it publishes fills and market data. Optimize for very low, predictable latency and strict fairness, and cover how you stay correct and recoverable.
blurb: The low-latency deterministic-core problem — a single-threaded order book with price-time priority, a sequencer for fairness, and event-sourced recovery.

rubric.label: Requirements gathering
rubric.description: Separates functional (limit/market orders, cancel/modify, price-time matching, market data feed) from non-functional (ultra-low + predictable latency, fairness, determinism, durability, auditability).

rubric.label: Clarifying questions
rubric.description: Asks about order types, instrument count, throughput and latency targets (and jitter/tail), fairness rules, regulatory/audit needs.

rubric.label: Order book & matching
rubric.description: Price-time priority, book data structure (price levels + FIFO queues), how a marketable order sweeps levels, partial fills, cancel/modify.

rubric.label: Low latency & determinism
rubric.description: Single-threaded deterministic core, in-memory book, avoiding GC/locks/syscalls on the hot path, kernel-bypass networking, mechanical sympathy, tail-latency focus.

rubric.label: Sequencer & fairness
rubric.description: A sequencer imposing one total order of events so matching is deterministic and fair; how arrival order is fixed; preventing queue-jumping.

rubric.label: High-level design
rubric.description: Gateways (auth/risk) -> sequencer -> matching engine (per instrument/shard) -> market-data + drop-copy publishers; event log for recovery.

rubric.label: Durability & recovery
rubric.description: Event sourcing / input log, hot-warm replicas fed the same ordered stream, deterministic replay, failover without losing or reordering orders.

rubric.label: Pre-trade risk & controls
rubric.description: Pre-trade risk checks off the hot path, circuit breakers / price bands, kill switch, self-trade prevention.

rubric.label: Scaling
rubric.description: Shard by instrument/symbol (independent books), scale gateways and market-data fan-out, keep each book single-threaded.

rubric.label: Bottlenecks
rubric.description: The single-threaded book as a throughput ceiling per symbol, market-data fan-out, tail-latency spikes (GC, contention).

rubric.label: Observability
rubric.description: Per-stage latency histograms (esp. tail), sequence-gap detection, book integrity checks, fairness/audit metrics.

functional_requirements: Accept limit and market orders, plus cancel/modify
Match by strict price-time priority; support partial fills
Maintain a live order book per instrument
Publish fills (execution reports / drop copy) and market data (L1/L2)
Enforce pre-trade risk and trading halts
nonfunctional_requirements: Ultra-low and predictable latency (low tail jitter, microseconds in the core)
Determinism: same inputs -> same outputs (for replay/recovery)
Durability and full auditability of every order/event
High availability with fast, correct failover
clarifying_questions: Which order types (limit, market, IOC/FOK, stop) must we support?
How many instruments, and expected orders/sec per symbol at peak?
Latency target — mean and, more importantly, tail/jitter?
Fairness model: strict price-time, pro-rata, or hybrid?
Co-located clients / kernel-bypass networking in scope?
qualifying_questions: Is deterministic replay a hard requirement for recovery?
Is tail latency (p99.99) or throughput the primary optimization target?
Single data center / co-lo, or geo-distributed?

estimations.throughput: A liquid symbol can see 100K-1M+ order events/sec at peak; the matching core must process each in well under a microsecond to hold latency.
estimations.book_size: Active price levels per symbol are modest (hundreds-thousands); the whole book fits in L2/L3 cache — keep it in memory, cache-friendly layout.
estimations.latency: Core matching target is sub-microsecond to a few microseconds; end-to-end wire-to-wire single-digit microseconds with kernel bypass. Jitter, not mean, is the enemy.
estimations.market_data: One trade fans out to thousands of subscribers -> market-data publishing, not matching, is often the real volume.

core_components: Matching engine per instrument shard (single-threaded, in-memory book)
data_model: order_book: bids/asks as price levels, each a FIFO queue of resting orders (price-time)
orders(order_id, symbol, side, price, qty, remaining, ts, seq)
events(seq, type[new/cancel/modify/trade], payload) — the durable input/event log
trades(trade_id, symbol, price, qty, buy_order, sell_order, seq, ts)
api_design: Order entry (binary protocol, e.g. FIX/ITCH-like): new/cancel/replace -> ack + seq
Execution reports / drop copy: fills, partials, rejects
Market data feed: L1 (top of book) and L2 (depth) incremental updates
Admin: halt symbol, set price bands, kill switch
reference.high_level_design: Clients connect to order-entry gateways that handle sessions, authentication, and pre-trade risk (off the matching hot path). Accepted orders flow to a sequencer that stamps every event with a monotonic sequence number, fixing one global (per-shard) total order — this is what makes matching deterministic and fair. The sequenced stream is durably logged and fed to the matching engine for that instrument, a single-threaded, in-memory order book that applies each event in sequence: a marketable order sweeps opposing price levels in price-time order, generating fills; non-marketable remainder rests in the book. Because the engine is deterministic over the ordered input, hot/warm replicas consuming the same log stay bit-identical and can take over on failure by replaying. Fills go to drop-copy/execution-report services; book changes go to the market-data publisher, which fans out L1/L2 updates to many subscribers. The core avoids GC, locks, and syscalls on the hot path (mechanical sympathy, pre-allocation, kernel-bypass NICs) to keep tail latency and jitter minimal.

deep_dives.probe: What data structure holds the book so that best-price lookup, insertion, and matching are all fast? Walk a marketable buy order sweeping multiple ask levels with partial fills and price-time priority within a level.
Why single-threaded? How do you keep the hot path free of GC pauses, locks, and syscalls, and why is p99.99 tail latency the metric that matters more than the mean?
How does a sequencer guarantee fairness and determinism? What stops a faster/closer client from jumping the queue, and how do you fix arrival order across multiple gateways?
The primary matching engine dies mid-session. How do warm replicas take over without losing, reordering, or double-executing orders? Explain the event-sourced replay from the sequenced log.
A single trade must reach thousands of subscribers with minimal, fair latency. How do you publish market data without the fan-out becoming the bottleneck or advantaging some subscribers?

Trades, positions, and order state must reach clearing, surveillance, and analytics systems reliably and in order. You must not slow the matching core. How do you propagate this — change data capture off a trade store, or consuming the immutable sequenced event log downstream — and why is dual-writing from the hot path dangerous?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions single thread or single-threaded or in-memory
followup_bank.question: How do you keep the hot path free of GC, locks, and syscalls, and how do you measure and control tail latency (p99.99) rather than the mean?
How does the sequencer fix arrival order across multiple gateways to guarantee fairness, and what happens if the sequencer itself fails?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions cache or in-memory or memory
followup_bank.question: The book lives in memory/cache — how do you keep it cache-friendly, and on a cold failover replica how do you avoid a stampede of replay before it's ready to trade?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions database or store or kafka or log
followup_bank.question: How do downstream systems (clearing, surveillance, analytics) consume trade/order state — CDC off a store or consuming the immutable event log — without dual-writing from the latency-critical core?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions replica or failover or recovery
followup_bank.question: Explain deterministic replay: how do replicas stay bit-identical, and how do you fail over without losing, reordering, or double-executing orders?

scaling: Shard by instrument/symbol — each book is independent and single-threaded
Scale order-entry gateways and pre-trade risk horizontally
Dedicate market-data publishing to its own fan-out tier
Co-locate and use kernel-bypass networking for latency
Keep per-symbol throughput within a single core's budget; add shards, not threads per book
bottlenecks: Sequencer as a per-shard serialization and failure point
tradeoffs: Single-threaded determinism (fair, replayable, per-core ceiling) vs multi-threaded throughput (faster, harder to keep fair/deterministic)
Strict price-time (simple, fair) vs pro-rata (favors size, complex)
In-memory speed vs durability (need event log + replicas for recovery)
Kernel-bypass/co-lo latency vs cost and operational complexity
alternative_solutions: LMAX Disruptor-style ring buffer + single-writer core
Pro-rata or hybrid matching for certain products
Sharded engines with a global sequencer per symbol group
observability: Per-stage latency histograms with tail focus (p99/p99.9/p99.99)
Fairness metrics (queue position honored), halt/circuit-breaker events
security: Strong session auth and per-participant entitlements
Pre-trade risk limits, price bands, and self-trade prevention
Immutable, tamper-evident audit log for surveillance/regulation
Isolation between participants; DoS protection at gateways
reference.reference_answer: A staff-level answer centers on a single-threaded, in-memory matching core applying a sequenced total order of events, giving determinism, fairness, and replayability. It designs the order book as price levels with FIFO (price-time) queues and walks a marketable order sweeping levels with partial fills. It puts auth and pre-trade risk on gateways off the hot path, uses a sequencer to fix arrival order (fairness) and to feed durable event-sourced logs that keep warm replicas bit-identical for fast, correct failover. It obsesses over tail latency/jitter (no GC, locks, or syscalls on the hot path; kernel bypass; mechanical sympathy), shards by symbol to scale, treats market-data fan-out as a first-class bottleneck, and propagates trades to clearing/surveillance by consuming the immutable log or CDC rather than dual-writing from the latency-critical core.

interviewer_notes: This is a staff-level, latency-first design; the signal is mechanical sympathy and determinism, not a sprawling microservice diagram. Insist on a single-threaded deterministic core and a sequenced total order — if they propose multi-threaded matching, probe how they preserve fairness and determinism. Make them design the order book concretely (price levels + FIFO) and walk a sweep with partial fills. Push tail latency (p99.99) over mean, and the no-GC/no-locks/no-syscalls hot path. If they mention in-memory/cache, probe cold-replica replay stampede on failover; if they mention a store/log/Kafka, hit the CDC-vs-dual-write probe for clearing/surveillance. Ensure recovery is event-sourced deterministic replay, not ad hoc.
